newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Gold market anxious, looks to IMF decision.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Gold market anxious, looks to IMF decision.

text.p: Tension ran high in the bullion market on Friday as the prospect that the International Monetary Fund would sell some of its gold reserves drew nearer.
Prices were virtually paralysed in early European trading in anticipation of an IMF board meeting later in the day, slated to discuss a proposal to gold to help pay for aid to poor nations.
Gold fixed slightly firmer at $382.50 an ounce, compared with $382.10 on Thursday afternoon.
The price of gold has sunk to two-month lows in recent days as big U.S. investment funds, expecting prices to sink on fears of fresh supplies of gold in the market, took short positions.
But despite the jittery mood, the market had already factored in a positive decision and was now poised to surge higher, a number of dealers said.
"After the news comes out, short covering by investment funds could help gold rebound, as long as there are few surprises in the plan," said a senior dealer at a Tokyo house.
A London-based bullion dealer noted, "If it's yea, prices are going to rocket, but even if it's nay, they market will still go up though not as much."
Bullion market analysts have said the proposed sale of about five million ounces of gold -- worth about $2 billion -- of the IMF's 104 million ounce reserve would be easily absorbed.
"In market terms, it's peanuts," said one dealer. In the 1970s the IMF auctioned off five times as much gold over a four-year period with little detrimental effect.
But the psychological effect of the upcoming decision nevertheless has sent a shiver of anxiety through the market, the dealer added.
Proponents of the plan, including the United States and Britain, have sought to assure the gold market that the effect of any sale would be minimal.
The Bank of England's deputy governer, Howard Davies, told the London Bullion Market Association on Thursday that Britain favoured a "phased" sale over time to minimise disruption.
"We believe it would be possible to sell this gold without important effect on the gold market," U.S. Deputy Treasury Lawrence Summers said early on Friday.
The debate over the IMF sales has dragged for two years with some member nations, notably Germany, voicing strong opposition.
But the IMF has recently indicated a willingness to go ahead with the proposal without German support.
"We expect to get an agreement that in the event of need the board will be willing to sell gold," IMF First Deputy Managing director Stanley Fischer said late on Thursday.
Britain's Davies said the debate was "finely balanced."
"We're not sure how the balance of opinion will end up. The Fund, for reasons we understand, will not force the issue unless they feel they have a majority," Davies said.

The rest of the precious metals were also closely watching for gold's reaction. Silver was five cents firmer at $5.06 an ounce after testing the key $5.00 support level on Thursday. Platinum was off $0.75 at $389.75.
